boss.briefing: Synthesis: make 5-methyl-1-hexanol from acetylene, one step per power node

questions.prompt: Bromocyclohexane is heated with KOH in ethanol. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Dehydrohalogenation: the base removes H and Br from neighboring carbons and leaves a C=C. The product is cyclohexene.

questions.prompt: 1-Methylcyclohexanol is treated with aqueous acid. What is the main product?
questions.explanation: Dehydration loses H₂O and gives the more substituted alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene (C=C in the ring next to the CH₃).

questions.prompt: Which reagents carry out this conversion?
questions.explanation: An alcohol loses water (dehydration) with acid. KOH/ethanol removes HX from an alkyl halide, not water from an alcohol.

questions.prompt: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane is heated with KOH in ethanol. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Loss of HBr gives 2-methylpropene. The double bond forms between the carbon that held Br and a neighboring carbon.

questions.prompt: Dehydrohalogenation and dehydration both make alkenes. What does each one remove?
questions.explanation: Alkyl halide − HX (base, e.g. KOH) → alkene. Alcohol − H₂O (acid, e.g. H₂SO₄) → alkene.
choices: Dehydrohalogenation removes HX; dehydration removes H₂O
Dehydrohalogenation removes X₂; dehydration removes H₂
Dehydrohalogenation removes H₂O; dehydration removes HX

questions.prompt: Cyclopentene reacts with Br₂. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Br₂ adds anti: the two Br atoms end up on opposite faces. trans-1,2-Dibromocyclopentane is the only product.

questions.prompt: Ethylene reacts with Cl₂. What is the product?
questions.explanation: One Cl adds to each carbon of the double bond: 1,2-dichloroethane.

questions.prompt: Cyclohexene reacts with Br₂ in water. What is the product?
questions.explanation: In water a halohydrin forms: Br on one carbon, OH on the other, added anti. The product is trans-2-bromocyclohexanol.

questions.prompt: 1-Methylcyclohexene reacts with Br₂ in water. Where do the Br and OH end up? (Stereochemistry not shown.)
questions.explanation: The OH goes to the more substituted carbon (the one with the CH₃) and the Br to the less substituted one: 2-bromo-1-methylcyclohexanol.

questions.prompt: Which reagent turns cyclohexene into trans-2-bromocyclohexanol?
questions.explanation: Water must be present to supply the OH. Br₂ in CH₂Cl₂ gives the dibromide instead.

questions.prompt: 1-Methylcyclopentene undergoes oxymercuration–demercuration. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Oxymercuration adds H and OH with Markovnikov regiochemistry: the OH goes to the more substituted carbon. 1-Methylcyclopentanol.

questions.prompt: 1-Methylcyclopentene undergoes hydroboration–oxidation. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Hydroboration is non-Markovnikov and syn: H and OH add to the same face, OH on the less substituted carbon. That puts CH₃ and OH trans: trans-2-methylcyclopentanol.

questions.prompt: 2-Methyl-2-pentene undergoes hydroboration–oxidation. What is the product?
questions.explanation: The OH goes to the less substituted alkene carbon: 2-methyl-3-pentanol (Worked Example 8.1a).

questions.prompt: 2-Methyl-2-pentene undergoes oxymercuration–demercuration. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Markovnikov hydration puts the OH on the more substituted carbon: 2-methyl-2-pentanol (Worked Example 8.1b).

questions.prompt: Which reagents give this alcohol from 3-methyl-3-hexene?
questions.explanation: The OH is on the less substituted carbon, so the alkene was hydrated non-Markovnikov: hydroboration–oxidation (Worked Example 8.2).

questions.prompt: 1-Butene is hydrated with aqueous acid. What forms?
questions.explanation: Markovnikov hydration gives 2-butanol. The starting alkene is achiral, so water adds equally to both faces: a racemic mixture.

questions.prompt: 1,2-Dimethylcyclohexene is hydrogenated. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Both H atoms add to the same face (syn) on the catalyst surface, so the two CH₃ groups end up cis: cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane.

questions.prompt: Cycloheptene reacts with meta-chloroperoxybenzoic acid (mCPBA). What is the product?
questions.explanation: A peroxyacid delivers one O atom to the double bond and gives an epoxide: 1,2-epoxycycloheptane.

questions.prompt: 1,2-Dimethylcyclopentene is treated with OsO₄, then NaHSO₃. What is the product?
questions.explanation: OsO₄ adds both OH groups to the same face (syn): cis-1,2-dimethyl-1,2-cyclopentanediol. Cleaving the C=C would need O₃ instead.

questions.prompt: Cyclohexene undergoes the Simmons–Smith reaction. What is the product?
questions.explanation: The zinc carbenoid adds a CH₂ across the double bond and closes a cyclopropane: bicyclo[4.1.0]heptane.

questions.prompt: Cyclohexene reacts with chloroform and KOH. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Base turns CHCl₃ into dichlorocarbene (:CCl₂), which adds to the C=C and gives a dichlorocyclopropane.

questions.prompt: Which reagents make this cis-1,2-diol?
questions.explanation: OsO₄ gives a cis diol. mCPBA stops at the epoxide; O₃ and acidic KMnO₄ break the C=C apart.

questions.prompt: Isopropylidenecyclohexane is treated with ozone, then zinc. What forms?
questions.explanation: Ozonolysis splits the C=C into two C=O groups: cyclohexanone and acetone.

questions.prompt: 1-Methylcyclohexene is treated with ozone, then zinc. What forms?
questions.explanation: The ring opens where the C=C was. The substituted carbon becomes a ketone and the CH becomes an aldehyde: 6-oxoheptanal.

questions.prompt: 1-Methylcyclohexene is treated with acidic KMnO₄. What forms?
questions.explanation: Acidic KMnO₄ cleaves the C=C like ozone, but any carbon that carried an H is oxidized further, to COOH: 6-oxoheptanoic acid.

questions.prompt: 3,7-Dimethyl-1-octene is treated with acidic KMnO₄. What forms?
questions.explanation: The terminal =CH₂ carbon is oxidized all the way to CO₂. The other carbon becomes a carboxylic acid: 2,6-dimethylheptanoic acid.

questions.prompt: Which alkene gives cyclopentanone and propanal on ozonolysis?
questions.explanation: Remove the two O atoms and join the two carbonyl carbons with a double bond: propylidenecyclopentane (Worked Example 8.3).

questions.prompt: With acidic KMnO₄, what does a terminal =CH₂ carbon become?
questions.explanation: KMnO₄ oxidizes as far as it can. A =CH₂ carbon has two H atoms and ends up as CO₂. (Ozonolysis would stop at CH₂O.)

questions.prompt: 1-Hexyne reacts with one equivalent of HBr. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Markovnikov addition: Br goes to the more substituted (internal) carbon: 2-bromo-1-hexene.

questions.prompt: 1-Hexyne reacts with two equivalents of HBr. What is the product?
questions.explanation: The second HBr adds Markovnikov to 2-bromo-1-hexene, putting both Br atoms on carbon 2: 2,2-dibromohexane.

questions.prompt: 1-Butyne reacts with one equivalent of Br₂. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Br₂ adds anti, so the two Br atoms end up trans: (E)-1,2-dibromo-1-butene. A second Br₂ would give the tetrabromide.

questions.prompt: 1-Hexyne is hydrated with HgSO₄ in aqueous acid. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Markovnikov addition of water gives an enol, which turns into the ketone: a methyl ketone, 2-hexanone.

questions.prompt: 1-Hexyne undergoes hydroboration–oxidation. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Non-Markovnikov: the O ends up on the terminal carbon. The enol becomes an aldehyde: hexanal.

questions.prompt: 3-Hexyne reacts with one equivalent of HCl. What is the product?
questions.explanation: H and Cl add anti, which here gives (Z)-3-chloro-3-hexene. A second HCl would give 3,3-dichlorohexane.

questions.prompt: Hydrating an unsymmetrical internal alkyne, R–C≡C–R′, with HgSO₄/H₃O⁺ gives…
questions.explanation: The OH can go to either alkyne carbon, so two different ketones form. That is why internal alkyne hydration is only useful when R = R′.

questions.prompt: 4-Octyne is hydrogenated with the Lindlar catalyst. What is the product?
questions.explanation: The Lindlar catalyst stops at the alkene and adds both H atoms to the same side: cis-4-octene.

questions.prompt: 5-Decyne is reduced with lithium in liquid ammonia. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Li/NH₃ gives the trans alkene: trans-5-decene.

questions.prompt: 4-Octyne is hydrogenated with Pd/C. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Pd/C does not stop at the alkene. Two equivalents of H₂ add and give the alkane, octane.

questions.prompt: Which reagents turn 2-hexyne into trans-2-hexene?
questions.explanation: Trans alkene from an alkyne: lithium in ammonia. Lindlar gives the cis alkene, and Pd/C goes all the way to the alkane.

questions.prompt: Which reagents turn 2-hexyne into cis-2-hexene?
questions.explanation: Cis alkene from an alkyne: H₂ with the poisoned Lindlar catalyst.

questions.prompt: 1,2-Dibromo-1,2-diphenylethane is heated with two equivalents of KOH. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Two eliminations of HBr from a vicinal dibromide give a triple bond: diphenylacetylene.

questions.prompt: 1-Hexyne is deprotonated with NaNH₂ and then treated with 1-bromobutane. What is the product?
questions.explanation: The acetylide anion replaces the Br and forms a new C–C bond. The butyl group goes on the alkyne end: 5-decyne.

questions.prompt: Propyne's acetylide anion (sodium salt) is mixed with bromocyclohexane, a secondary alkyl halide. What happens?
questions.explanation: With secondary (and tertiary) alkyl halides the acetylide acts as a base: it removes H and Br, giving cyclohexene back propyne. Alkylation works with primary halides.

questions.prompt: Which base is strong enough to remove the H from a terminal alkyne (R–C≡C–H)?
questions.explanation: Terminal alkynes are weak acids (pKa about 25). The amide ion, NH₂⁻, is a strong enough base; hydroxide is not.

questions.prompt: How would you make 1-pentyne from acetylene?
questions.explanation: Make the acetylide with NaNH₂, then alkylate with a primary halide that carries the three extra carbons, 1-bromopropane. 2-Bromopropane is secondary and would mostly eliminate.

questions.prompt: Step 1: Turn acetylene into its acetylide anion. Which reagent?
questions.explanation: Only a very strong base such as NaNH₂ removes the alkyne H.

questions.prompt: Step 2: Which alkyl halide gives 5-methyl-1-hexyne?
questions.explanation: The halide must be primary and carry the five carbons the target still needs. 1-Bromo-3-methylbutane fits; the secondary halide would eliminate.

questions.prompt: Step 3: Reduce 5-methyl-1-hexyne to 5-methyl-1-hexene. Which reagents?
questions.explanation: Lindlar stops at the alkene. Pd/C would go all the way to the alkane.

questions.prompt: Step 4: Turn 5-methyl-1-hexene into the primary alcohol, 5-methyl-1-hexanol. Which reagents?
questions.explanation: A primary alcohol from a terminal alkene needs non-Markovnikov hydration: hydroboration–oxidation. Markovnikov methods would give the secondary alcohol.
